task: Write one sentence of your own using the word nebulous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know nebulous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The band's plan to 'reinvent our sound' stayed nebulous through three rehearsals that sounded exactly like the old sound.
A fuzzy plan has real edges that blur here and there; nebulous goes further - the plan is all cloud and no outline.
A hazy memory keeps its outline half in view behind the mist; nebulous means even the outline is gone - nothing but vapor remains.

Vague is the everyday, all-purpose word for anything not pinned down — a vague answer, a vague promise, a vague sense of direction. Nebulous is stronger and more pointed: it says a plan or idea is all cloud, with no outline at all for anyone to grab.

Indistinct belongs to perception: something real is there, but the eye or ear cannot quite make out its edges — a coastline in fog, a voice through a wall. Nebulous points at the thing itself, saying the idea or plan has never taken a settled form.

Nebulous means vaguely defined, cloudy.

Since fifth grade Amir has carried a nebulous dream to 'work with the ocean' - some years it is dolphins, some years ships, one memorable year 'waves in general.' The wish gleams, drifts, and never gains enough outline to choose a single class by.
Nebulous is exact because the dream never takes definable form: no job title, no course list, no first step.
It is not ambiguous - there are not two clear versions to pick between - and it is not a precise idea awaiting examples.
It is a cloud that shines and will not condense.
Nebulous is the cloud-word for ideas, plans, and promises that never take shape.
Amorphous is its cluster-mate for physical things and organizations; ambiguity means two sharp readings, not none; and an abstraction can be perfectly precise.
Calling a plan nebulous is a criticism: it says there is nothing yet to grab.

For forty years, director Mara Voss kept announcing the same project: a film she called simply 'The Crossing.' What the film actually was remained nebulous for her entire career.
In interviews she offered moods -- 'a story about thresholds,' 'water, but not the sea' -- while declining to name a plot, a period, or a single character.

Studios that asked for a page of outline received, one executive recalled, 'weather instead.' When her notebooks were opened after her death, archivists found hundreds of pages of images and not one scene: the project had never taken a form even she could state.
